To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the laser ablation of solid metal targets in liquid leads to the formation of a superheated molte layer at the water-metal target interface, which in turn leads to the formation and expansion of a low density metal-water supercritical mixture, which is the precursor for the cavitation bubble formation, and that the nanoparticle formation is driven by two distinct mechanisms: (1) nanoparticle formation in a supercritical water environment and (2) nanoparticle formation through the breakup of a superheating metal

the laser ablation of the metal film in water leads to the formation of two distinct populations of nanoparticles, the first one with the characteristic sizes in the 10 nm range, and the second one with the sizes in the 100 nm range.

the formation of nanoparticles during laser ablation of metals in water is facilitated by (1) the rapid deceleration and cooling of the ablation plume in water, (2) the rapid formation of a dense metal-water mixing layer at the water-metal interface and (3) the breakup of the molten metal layer due to the Rayleigh–Taylor instability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of an integrated atomistic simulation framework that can be used for a detailed understanding of the mechanisms of the laser nanoparticle generation.
atomistic simulation of laser ablated nanoparticles in water.
fundamental mechanisms of nanoparticle generation and growth in laser ablation in liquid environments.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the atomistic modeling is a very promising approach for the study of fundamental mechanisms of laser ablation in liquid environments and can be a useful tool for rational design of nanoparticle synthesis.

the simulations provide a detailed description of the complex processes occurring at the interface between a supercritical water medium and the metal vapor plume generated in the laser ablation process.

the simulations presented here are consistent with experimental observations, but the agreement is far from being perfect and the simulations are still far from being able to predict the nanoparticle size distribution quantitatively.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the atomistic simulations of the laser ablated metal target in liquid environment provide a detailed insight into the fundamental processes of the ablation plume deceleration, cavitation bubble formation, and nanoparticle generation.

atomistic simulations are able to capture the fundamental physics of the nanoparticle generation in laser ablation in liquid and predict the characteristic size of the nanoparticles as well as their formation mechanism.
we developed a model for atomistic simulation of laser ablated nanoparticles that can be used as a predictive tool for optimization of nanoparticle synthesis in laser ablation of metals in liquids.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the atomistic simulation can be used for a detailed analysis of the key processes that govern the formation and evolution of the ablation plume in laser ablation in liquid and for a quantitative characterization of the mechanisms of the nanoplasmonic nanoparticle formation.
the laser ablation of solid targets in water is a complex process involving the formation of multiple phases and the emergence of complex hydrodynamic instabilities.
the atomistic simulation of laser ablations in liquids can provide insights into the fundamental mechanisms of nanoparticle generation that cannot be captured by macroscopic continuum models.
